newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivory Coast holds violence-delayed polls Sunday.
newsitem.headline: Ivory Coast holds violence-delayed polls Sunday.

text.p: Ivory Coast wraps up its second multi-party elections on Sunday with by-elections in an opposition stronghold which saw ethnic and political bloodshed during its turbulent 1995 presidential election.

Veteran opposition leader Laurent Gbagbo will try to regain the seat he held in the previous parliament but was unable to contest in the country's November 1995 parliamentary poll after the interior ministry postponed polling there.

The by-elections, for eight seats in and around Gbagbo's Gagnoa stronghold in the west and in the north and east, will not alter the balance of power in parliament where President Henri Konan Bedie's supporters enjoy a huge majority.

The postponement in and around Gagnoa followed clashes between indigenous Bete supporters of Gbabgo's Ivorian Popular Front and migrant farmers of Bedie's Baoule tribe in which 25 people were killed. Most of the dead were Baoule.

Laurent Languy, standing against Gbagbo under the colours of Bedie's Democratic Party, was quoted in Saturday's edition of the government newspaper Fraternite Matin as saying that his supporters were afraid following the events of 1995.
La Voie, Gbagbo's party newspaper, spoke of a heavy deployment of security forces, describing Gagnoa as a town under a state of siege.
A total of 18 candidates will contest Sunday's polls in and around Gagnoa and in Korhogo and Seguela in the north and Adzope in the east. Municipal reruns will be held in four northern districts.
Ivory Coast, the world's top cocoa producer, held its first multi-party elections in 1990.
